subject: math
cluster: Use random sampling to draw inferences about a population
intro: These problems ask you to apply the definitions of sampling. For each one, classify the sampling method into a named category, identify the specific source of bias and its cause, or decide which of two plans is more representative. Remember that a method looks reasonable does not make the sample representative.

items.prompt: A radio host asks listeners to call in and say whether they support a new highway. Of the $300$ callers, $200$ say yes. Name the type of sampling method this is and explain why it may not represent all residents.
items.answer: It is a voluntary response sample; only people who chose to call in are included, so people with strong opinions are overrepresented and the sample is not representative.

steps: The host did not select anyone; people decided on their own whether to call. That is the definition of a voluntary response sample.
In a voluntary response sample, people with the strongest feelings (often those who are angry or very enthusiastic) are the most likely to participate.
Because participation is self-selected rather than random, the $\frac{200}{300}$ who said yes may not reflect the views of all residents.
Method: voluntary response sample. It may be biased toward people who feel strongly about the highway.

items.prompt: A manager wants to know what all $500$ factory workers think of the cafeteria. She stands at the cafeteria door at lunch and surveys the workers who come to eat. Identify the source of bias in this plan and state its cause.
items.answer: The plan has self-selection (location) bias: only workers who actually use the cafeteria are surveyed, so workers who dislike it and eat elsewhere are left out.

steps: The population is all $500$ workers, but the sample is taken only from people already at the cafeteria.
Workers who think the cafeteria is bad may avoid it entirely and bring their own lunch, so they have no chance of being surveyed.
This makes the sample favor workers who like the cafeteria.
Source of bias: sampling only an unrepresentative subgroup (cafeteria users). Cause: the survey location excludes workers who avoid the cafeteria.

items.prompt: To estimate the average height of all students at a middle school, a coach measures every member of the basketball team. Classify this sampling method and explain whether it will give a representative estimate.
items.answer: It is a convenience sample of an unrepresentative subgroup; basketball players tend to be taller than average, so the estimate will be too high and is not representative.

steps: The coach chose an easy-to-reach group already gathered for practice, so this is a convenience sample.
The population is all students, but basketball players are not typical of all students with respect to height.
Players are generally taller than the average student, so the sample mean height will be biased upward.
The estimate will not be representative; a method that gives every student an equal chance would be needed.

items.prompt: A school has $800$ students. To pick a sample, an administrator writes every student's name on a slip, places all slips in a bin, mixes them, and draws $60$ slips. Classify this sampling method and explain why it tends to be representative.
items.answer: It is a simple random sample; every student has an equal chance of being drawn, so the sample tends to mirror the whole population.

steps: Every one of the $800$ students has a slip, and the draw is made after mixing, so each student has an equal chance of selection.
Equal chance of selection for every member is the definition of a simple random sample.
Random selection means no subgroup is systematically favored, so the sample tends to reflect the population.
Method: simple random sample. It tends to be representative because selection is random and unbiased.

items.prompt: A quality inspector checks every $20$th phone that comes off an assembly line. Classify this sampling method by name and state whether it is random or non-random.
items.answer: It is a systematic sample; because phones are inspected at a fixed interval rather than chosen at random, it is generally treated as non-random (though it can be representative if the order is unrelated to quality).

steps: The inspector uses a fixed pattern, every $20$th phone, so this is a systematic sample.
In a systematic sample, members are chosen by a rule (a set interval), not by random draw, so it is classified as non-random.
It can still be representative if the order of phones is unrelated to any quality pattern.
Method: systematic sample. Non-random, since selection follows a fixed interval rather than chance.

items.prompt: A city wants opinions on a new park from all residents. Plan A: survey people picked from a randomly drawn list of registered addresses. Plan B: survey everyone at the dog park on Saturday. Which plan gives the more representative sample, and why?
items.answer: Plan A is more representative, because addresses are drawn at random so every resident can be selected, while Plan B reaches only dog owners who visit that park.

steps: Plan A draws from a list of all addresses at random, giving residents an equal chance of selection.
Plan B surveys only people at the dog park, an unrepresentative subgroup that overrepresents dog owners.
Random selection (Plan A) avoids favoring any subgroup, while a convenience location (Plan B) introduces bias.
Plan A is more representative because it is a random sample of all residents, not just dog-park visitors.

items.prompt: A survey question reads: 'Don't you agree that our wonderful library deserves more funding?' Identify the source of bias in this survey and explain its cause.
items.answer: The question is a leading question; its wording pushes respondents toward agreeing, so the responses are biased toward 'yes.'

steps: Bias here comes from the wording of the question, not from who is sampled.
Words like 'wonderful' and 'Don't you agree' steer the respondent toward a particular answer.
A leading question pressures people to give the answer the survey expects, inflating agreement.
Source of bias: a leading question. Cause: the wording is slanted and encourages a 'yes' response.

items.prompt: A reporter wants to know how all shoppers at a large mall feel about parking. She interviews the first $25$ people who walk past her near the food court. Classify this sampling method and explain why it may be biased.
items.answer: It is a convenience sample; only shoppers near the food court at that moment can be chosen, so shoppers in other areas or at other times are excluded, which may bias the results.

steps: The reporter chose whoever was easiest to reach at one spot, so this is a convenience sample.
The population is all mall shoppers, but only people near the food court at that time had a chance to be picked.
Shoppers who parked far away or shop at other times are systematically left out.
Method: convenience sample. It may be biased because it samples only one location at one time, not all shoppers.

items.prompt: A teacher wants to know the favorite subject of all $400$ seventh graders. Plan A: survey the $30$ students in the school chess club. Plan B: assign each student a number from $1$ to $400$ and use a random number generator to choose $30$ numbers. Which plan is less biased, and why?
items.answer: Plan B is less biased; the random number generator gives every student an equal chance, while Plan A samples only chess-club members, who may favor certain subjects.

steps: Plan A surveys only chess-club members, a subgroup whose interests may differ from typical students.
Plan B assigns numbers to all $400$ students and chooses randomly, so each student has an equal chance.
Random selection avoids favoring any subgroup, while the chess club is an unrepresentative subgroup.
Plan B is less biased because it is a simple random sample of all seventh graders.

items.prompt: A company emails a satisfaction survey to all customers and uses only the responses from customers who choose to reply. Classify this sampling method and explain why the results may be biased.
items.answer: It is a voluntary response sample; only customers who chose to reply are counted, so customers with strong opinions are overrepresented and the results may be biased.

steps: Although the email reaches all customers, only those who decide to reply are included, so the sample is self-selected.
Self-selected participation defines a voluntary response sample.
Customers who are very happy or very unhappy are more motivated to respond than those with neutral views.
Method: voluntary response sample. Results may be biased toward customers with strong opinions.

items.prompt: To learn how all $1{,}200$ employees commute to work, a researcher surveys only the people waiting at the bus stop outside the building. Identify the specific source of bias and explain its cause.
items.answer: The sample suffers from sampling an unrepresentative subgroup: it includes only bus riders, so employees who drive, bike, or walk are excluded, biasing results toward bus use.

steps: The population is all $1{,}200$ employees, but the sample comes only from a bus stop.
People at a bus stop almost all commute by bus, so other commuters have no chance of being surveyed.
This overrepresents bus riders and underrepresents drivers, bikers, and walkers.
Source of bias: sampling only an unrepresentative subgroup. Cause: the bus-stop location excludes all non-bus commuters.

items.prompt: A pollster surveys $1{,}000$ people but interviews only people leaving an expensive restaurant to ask how all city residents feel about raising the sales tax. The pollster says the sample is fine because $1{,}000$ is a large number. Is the pollster's reasoning correct? Explain.
items.answer: No; a large sample size does not fix bias. The people leaving an expensive restaurant are an unrepresentative subgroup, so the sample is biased no matter how large it is.

steps: The pollster argues that size alone makes the sample good, but size does not remove bias.
Everyone surveyed comes from one expensive restaurant, an unrepresentative subgroup of higher-spending people.
Their views on a sales tax may differ from those of all residents, so the sample is biased.
The reasoning is incorrect: a representative sample requires unbiased (random) selection, not just a large count.

items.prompt: A librarian wants opinions on weekend hours from all library members. Plan A: hand a paper survey to every member who visits on Saturday. Plan B: randomly select members from the full membership list and call them. Explain which plan is more likely to give a representative sample.
items.answer: Plan B is more representative; it randomly selects from all members, while Plan A reaches only members who already visit on Saturdays.

steps: Plan A only surveys Saturday visitors, who already prefer or are available on weekends, an unrepresentative subgroup.
Plan B selects randomly from the full membership list, giving every member an equal chance.
Random selection from the whole list avoids favoring weekend visitors.
Plan B is more likely to be representative because it is a random sample of all members.

items.prompt: A student stands in the school's main hallway and surveys every fifth person who walks by during passing period to learn what all students think of the new schedule. Classify the sampling method and state whether you would expect it to be representative.
items.answer: It is a systematic sample (every fifth person); because passing-period traffic in the main hallway includes a broad mix of students chosen by a fixed rule, it can be fairly representative as long as the order of students is unrelated to their opinions.

steps: Choosing every fifth person uses a fixed interval, so this is a systematic sample.
Systematic sampling is non-random in selection but can approximate a representative sample.
If students passing in the main hallway are a broad mix and their order has nothing to do with their schedule opinions, the sample can be fairly representative.
Method: systematic sample. It can be reasonably representative unless the order of students is linked to their views.

items.prompt: Two students each survey classmates about a field trip. One says, 'Would you like to go on an exciting trip to the amazing science museum?' The other says, 'Do you want the class field trip to go to the science museum?' Identify which question is biased, name the type of bias, and explain the cause.
items.answer: The first question is biased; it is a leading question because words like 'exciting' and 'amazing' steer respondents toward saying yes, while the second question is neutral.

steps: Compare the wording of the two questions; the difference is in tone, not in who is asked.
The first uses persuasive words ('exciting,' 'amazing') that encourage a 'yes' answer.
The second simply asks the question without slanted wording, so it is neutral.
The first question is biased. Type: leading question. Cause: its emotionally loaded wording pushes respondents toward agreeing.
